input: This cost review takes a detailed look at the transport costs associated with a returns flow, with a particular focus on understanding the overall annual expenditure involved in moving returned goods through the operation. Based on the available figures, the returns flow involves a distance of 569 km per trip at a cost of $0.93 per km, and a total of 592 trips per year is carried out. When these elements are brought together, the annual transport cost is $313k. It is important to note that these costs are drawn from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, which provides a recent and relevant basis for the review. In addition, empty running is included in the trip count, meaning that the reported number of trips reflects not only the loaded movements but also the unloaded movements that form part of the overall returns operation. Overall, the review provides a clear picture of the current cost position for the returns flow, based on invoiced activity over the period considered. This framing is useful because it keeps the distance travelled, the rate charged and the frequency of travel together in a single annual figure, rather than treating each element in isolation. It also means that the review reflects the operation as it was actually invoiced during the period, including movements that did not themselves carry returned goods but were nevertheless part of the overall transport activity.

The three components of the figure are the distance per trip, the rate per kilometre, and the number of trips in the year. Each comes from the invoice record for the same period, which keeps the annual cost on one consistent basis. Any comparison with another period or another carrier needs the same trip definition, the same treatment of empty running, and the same invoice basis before the totals can be set against each other. The annual figure should therefore be read as an operating total, not as a price for the loaded leg alone. Its basis is activity-based: distance, rate and trip frequency are all taken from the same invoice period, and the unloaded portion of the work is inside the total rather than estimated separately.
